claims.text: Existing refractory high-entropy alloys for energetic structural applications can combine very high strength with significant impact-induced chemical energy release.
The untreated refractory HEA baseline suffers from limited ductility.
The untreated refractory HEA baseline exhibits inhomogeneous plastic deformation.
Adding approximately 5–10 at.% W to a refractory HEA can improve its mechanical properties.
A minor W addition induces nanoscale, uniformly dispersed, ductile precipitates in refractory HEAs.
Changing W content can control the phase constitution or phase ratio of a Ti-Zr-Mo-based refractory HEA.
The proposed W-induced precipitates alter the refractory HEA's stacking-fault energy.
The proposed precipitates provide precipitation hardening that maintains high strength.
The proposed precipitates increase beneficial dislocation mobility.
The proposed precipitates encourage mechanical twinning.
Precipitation hardening together with increased dislocation mobility or twinning produces more homogeneous plastic deformation and greater ductility.
Relative to an untreated refractory HEA, the W-modified alloy will have increased ductility.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the W-modified alloy will deform more uniformly.
The W-modified refractory HEA will retain high yield and ultimate strengths.
The W-modified refractory HEA will retain impact-induced chemical energy-release capacity.
The strength reduction caused by the intervention will be less than approximately 5–10% relative to baseline.
A W-containing Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 refractory HEA can retain high strength and substantial fracture strain under dynamic loading near 3000 s−1.
The proposed benefit requires processing that produces a nanoscale, uniform precipitate dispersion without a continuous soft-phase network.
Precipitate coarsening or formation of a continuous soft-phase network can eliminate the proposed benefits.
Adverse interactions between the precipitates and dynamic impact behavior can prevent the expected improvement.
